newsitem.title: UK: SOCCER-ENGLAND AND ITALY POISED FOR CRUCIAL QUALIFIER.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-ENGLAND AND ITALY POISED FOR CRUCIAL QUALIFIER.

text.p: Nothing less than victory over Italy on Wednesday will convince millions of fans and a traditionally critical media that coach Glenn Hoddle is leading England along the road that leads directly to next year's World Cup finals.

The match is being treated as if it was a major final itself, with thousands of words, newspaper supplements and magazine articles analysing every minor detail from the condition of Alan Shearer's back injury to Paolo Maldini's "sculpted, complex and sophisticated cheekbones."
For once, the hype is probably justified.

Wednesday's match -- and the return in Rome in October -- are the only ones in the entire European qualifying programme to be played between two former World champions and with both England and Italy protecting 100 per cent records going into the game, something has to give.

The arrival of Italian stars like Fabrizio Ravanelli, Gianfranco Zola and Gianluca Vialli in the English premier league have added another dimension to the match, the outcome of which will have a huge bearing on which country qualifies automatically from the group for France 98 and which might have to go through the play-offs.
Hoddle has enjoyed a superb start as England coach with three wins in his opening three matches against Moldova, Poland and Georgia.

But victory over the Italians would add tremendously to his own personal prestige as a coach and go a long way in confirming that England really are returning to the elite of world soccer after reaching the semifinals of Euro 96 last summer.

England were boosted on Tuesday with the news that captain Shearer and midfielder Paul Gascoigne appeared to have shaken off injury worries that put their participation in doubt, although the playing chances of centreback Tony Adams (ankle) and Italy-based midfielder Paul Ince (thigh strain) were rated as only 50-50.
Depending on whether they are fit or not will determine exactly what team Hoddle will select and to a lesser degree what formation he will play.

England will have to be patient, but at the same time must go searching for goals. Hoddle must decide whether to play Shearer alone up front and supported by more withdrawn players or whether he will be partnered in attack by his Newcastle team mate Les Ferdinand. David Beckham, 21, having an outstanding season with Manchester United is capable of scoring from close or long range, as is Liverpool's Steve McManaman. Arsenal's Paul Merson has also been in excellent form this season and if Gascoigne is 100 per cent fit and plays well and if Ince recovers fitness, the England midfield seems capable of competing all the way with the Italians for control of the game.
Italy are playing their second match under new coach Cesare Maldini, who has succeeded the unpopular Arrigo Sacchi and is expected to play a 3-5-2 formation, solidly built on defence.
He used that set-up when Italy beat Northern Ireland 2-0 in a friendly in his first match in charge last month and there is no doubt the Italians will respect England as much as England respect them.
Italy were training at Wembley Stadium on Tuesday morning and Maldini was not expected to name his side until Wednesday.
Vialli, out of the squad, is definitely not playing, but his countrymen who do pull on their blue shirts on Wednesday night will certainly give England a huge test.

England are well aware of Zola's devastating accuracy from freekicks around the box, and as Adams said this week: "Look at the Italian team and you will be hard pressed to find a weak link anywhere. They are all talented, all special and we will have to be very patient to break them down. One mistake and they can finish you."

Hoddle himself says: "You don't get an extra point for beating Italy." That may be true, but you do get a massive psychological lift and at this stage of the campaign, that is a very nice bonus to have.
